w: Edward Partridge bought this 63-acre parcel in 1831, after Joseph Smith said a revelation named it the site of a coming 'City of Zion' temple. Ownership is still split: a 2.5-acre grassy field held by the Church of Christ (Temple Lot), and 61 larger acres held by the Community of Christ.

n: Kauffman Center for the Performing Arts
w: Opened in 2011 without taxpayer funding, this two-venue hall gave Kansas City's ballet, opera and symphony a permanent home after decades sharing the Lyric Theatre eight blocks north. The 1,800-seat Kauffman Theatre and 1,600-seat Helzberg Hall anchor a redeveloped stretch of downtown.

n: Harry S. Truman Presidential Library and Museum
w: Harry Truman is buried on the grounds of this library on US Highway 24 in Independence, alongside his wife Bess and daughter Margaret. Created under the 1955 Presidential Libraries Act, it was the first presidential library of its kind -- the template for the thirteen the National Archives now administers.

n: National Collegiate Basketball Hall of Fame
w: Part of the T-Mobile Center's College Basketball Experience, this hall exists purely to honor men's college basketball, distinct from the Naismith Memorial Hall in Springfield. Its founding class, inducted in 2006, ran to roughly 180 honorees, among them Oscar Robertson, Bill Russell, Dean Smith and John Wooden.

n: Kansas City Power and Light Building
w: KCP&L president Joseph Porter built this Art Deco tower in 1931 partly to create new jobs downtown. It was the tallest building west of the Mississippi River until Seattle's Space Needle overtook it in 1962, and its illuminated lantern crown still appears on branding for the Power & Light District that took its name.

w: Founded December 5, 1873, this is the oldest public library system in the Kansas City metro. Its Central Library holds the Missouri Valley Room -- original photographs, maps, postcards and directories tracing the city's history -- alongside the Ramos Collection on African-American history and culture.

w: This multi-purpose civic hall opened in 1935 in a blend of Streamline Moderne and Art Deco -- the curved lines and geometric detailing typical of the era's public buildings, still standing in downtown Kansas City nearly a century on.

w: Completed July 3, 1869, this was the first permanent rail crossing of the Missouri River, turning the young City of Kansas -- renamed Kansas City twenty years later -- into a major rail hub almost overnight. A tornado later destroyed it; a second Hannibal Bridge was rebuilt on virtually the same spot.

Destroyed by a tornado; rebuilt as the Second Hannibal Bridge

w: Dug up to 160 feet into a limestone mine, this business park bills itself as the World's Largest Underground Business Complex -- 14 million square feet of tunnels holding the Postal Service's stamp operations, an EPA training center, and National Archives storage, at a steady 65-70 degrees year-round.
